lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Options and Consent
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Diego Leonel George Wached | Lesson 9 -- Options and Consent
lesson.grammar_point: second conditional and modals of possibility

listenings.text: People assume this station is about being nice, and it is not. It is about whether the patient could have chosen. There are three things I watch for, and the first one nobody believes until they see themselves on video. Candidates present the second option in less detail and with less warmth than the first. Every single time. They spend ninety seconds on one and twenty on the other, and they never say anything untrue, and the patient walks out having been steered, and neither of them noticed it happen. Give both options the same time and the same care, or you have decided for them. The second is the phrase it is your decision. Said on its own, at the end, that is not autonomy, that is abandonment. The patient asked what you would do. Refusing to answer is not neutrality: it is leaving somebody alone with a choice they do not have the training to make. Say what you would do, say why, and then say clearly that it is your reasoning and not a decision. And the third thing is one question, and it is the one that goes missing most often. Is there a concern you have not mentioned. The real reason a treatment gets refused almost never arrives on its own. Somebody has to ask for it.

I had been to four appointments before that one, and in all four I was given a plan and asked whether I agreed. That is not the same as choosing, and I did not have the words for the difference until it happened. He put two things in front of me. He said, if you chose the cream it would take about twelve weeks, and it is reversible, if it does not suit you we stop. And then he said the same amount about the tablets, the same detail, including the part that worried me. And then I asked him what he would do, which I had never dared ask anybody, and he said: in your position I would probably start with the cream, because it is reversible. And then, straight after, that it was his reasoning and not a decision. Those two sentences together are the reason I trusted him. And then he told me to take the week and talk it through at home, which had never happened before either. It was the first time a decision did not have to be made in the room. I chose the tablets in the end. But I chose them.

extra_audio.text: There are two reasonable options, and waiting is a third. If you chose the cream, it would take about twelve weeks. If you went for the tablets, we would need a blood test first. That is the trade-off: speed against monitoring. In your position I would probably start with the cream, but that is my reasoning, not a decision. Is there a concern you have not mentioned?
